#644. Werner Holzer Prize awarded to Katja Gloger and DW's Jaafar Abdul Karim

DW journalist Jaafar Abdul Karim and Russia correspondent Katja Gloger have been awarded the prestigious Werner Holzer Prize for international journalism.

At a time when press freedom is under pressure and international newsrooms are shrinking, the Werner Holzer Prize celebrates a profession that many consider indispensable to democracy: foreign correspondence.

Presented in honor of Werner Holzer, the veteran reporter and former editor-in-chief of the German daily newspaper Frankfurter Rundschau, this year's award coincided with what would have been his 100th birthday. Holzer spent decades reporting from some of the world's most important hot spots and championing international journalism.

At the award ceremony in Frankfurt's Römer, the city's historic town hall, Mayor Mike Josef recalled that fundamental rights such as freedom of speech and freedom of the press were first enshrined for all Germans by the Frankfurt Parliament in the nearby Paulskirche in 1848.

To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

The 2026 winners reflect the breadth and ambition of the award. First prize went to Katja Gloger, a veteran Russia correspondent who moved to Moscow in 1989 and accompanied Vladimir Putin during the early years of his presidency.

In her recent nonfiction book, "The Failure: An Investigative Report of Germany's Russia Policy," Gloger and co-author Georg Mascolo offer a searing critique of the misjudgments and illusions that shaped German policy toward Russia for decades.

Second prize was awarded to DW journalist and presenter Jaafar Abdul Karim. His talk show JaafarTalk reaches millions of viewers across the Arab world and in Germany. Whether in Tunis, Beirut or Cairo, Abdul Karim tackles subjects that are often considered taboo.

A research grant went to freelance journalist Luise Land, whose current project explores why her German-Namibian family still owns extensive landholdings in Namibia today. By tracing that history, she examines the enduring legacy of the genocide against the Herero and Nama peoples by German colonial forces in the early 20th century.

"Katja Gloger is one of the leading foreign policy reporters. For decades, she has been among the foremost experts on Russia and speaks out on uncomfortable truths," the jury stated on Friday, explaining its decision to honor Gloger. "Like almost no one else, she has gained access to the very heart of the Kremlin's power elite — from Mikhail Gorbachev to Vladimir Putin."

At the prize-giving ceremony, Gloger delivered a passionate plea for more journalism — and more international coverage — in the German press. "We must defend trustworthy, reliable and fact-based journalism with everything in our power," she said.

To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

Gloger worked for Reporters Without Borders for 12 years. "The latest rankings show that only one in 100 people can get their information from free, independent journalism and a free, independent press. That shows what's at stake," she said.

The prize winner also said she would dedicate the award to journalists in exile and to her colleagues at Novaya Gazeta, the independent Russian newspaper long known for its critical reporting on the Kremlin. Earlier this week, the paper was forced to shut down its operations in Russia and leave its Moscow newsroom.

In his acceptance speech, Jaafar Abdul Karim said journalism has become more challenging and exhausting than ever. The DW host spoke of hatred and incitement, attacks and threats, both online and offline, in the regions he reports on as well as in Germany.

Such pressure, he said, takes a personal toll — yet giving up is not an option. "When I listen to my heart, I know I have to keep going," he said. The answer, he argued, is a form of journalism that fosters dialogue, embraces multiple perspectives and helps bridge divides rather than deepen them.

"I firmly believe in the power of dialogue, today more than ever. That's why we must talk to one another. Even when it gets difficult. Even when we disagree. Or perhaps precisely because of that," he said.

Listening doesn't mean agreeing, and understanding doesn't mean being in agreement. "Especially now, in times of polarization, when those who believe they're always right are often the loudest, we as journalists have a special responsibility. When everyone is just shouting into their own bubbles or communities, we need journalists who connect these bubbles with one another," he said.

The jury praised Abdul Karim for creating programs at DW that reach millions of young people across the Arab world and in Germany. "His journalism fosters dialogue between countries, between generations, and between religions. He has set new standards," the jury stated.

So far in 2026, JaafarTalk has already garnered more than 1.1 billion views across all platforms, and its community has grown to more than 9 million followers. Its motto: "Diversity fosters dialogue."

"We need fact-based journalism that promotes dialogue and reflects the diversity of our society," Abdul Karim stressed. "By that, I mean an honest and open dialogue in which we do not look away or remain silent. On the contrary, we must take a clear stand against racism, antisemitism, Islamophobia, discrimination, sexism, and hate speech — no matter which side they come from."

#643. NASA smashed into an asteroid. Now Hera has revealed a strange new world

The European Space Agency's (ESA) Hera spacecraft has captured its first close-up image of the Didymos asteroid system, offering scientists a surprising new perspective on the site of NASA's historic asteroid deflection experiment.

On September 26, 2022, NASA's DART spacecraft deliberately crashed into Dimorphos, the smaller of the two asteroids in the system. Hera's latest image provides a look at its larger companion, Didymos, from a side that scientists had not previously seen in such detail.

The image was taken from a distance of 60 km using Hera's monochromatic Asteroid Framing Camera, which captures images in black and white. Although most of Dimorphos, which measures 151 m across, is concealed in shadow, the much larger Didymos, with a diameter of 780 m, is clearly visible.

A Surprisingly Different Side of Asteroid Didymos

"The first thing we said was wow!" observes Hera Principal Investigator Patrick Michel, Director of Research at CNRS / Observatoire de la Côte d'Azur. "This is the other side of Didymos from the one that DART's camera showed us shortly before impact, so this feels like looking at a whole new world.

"This side of Didymos has the same central ridge along its equator that we saw before, but otherwise appears very different, with multiple boulders and craters and what look like patterns of grooves or ridges."

The newly revealed terrain raises intriguing questions about how the asteroid's surface developed and whether NASA's collision with Dimorphos may have left traces on its larger neighbor.

When DART struck Dimorphos, the impact sent material flying into space. Scientists believe some of that debris may have traveled across the roughly 1 km separating the two asteroids and reached Didymos. Determining whether this material contributed to the features now visible on its surface will be an important part of Hera's investigation.

ESA's Hera mission scientist Michael Kueppers adds: "Since we expect a lot of impact-ejected material to have made it across the approximately 1 km of space from Dimorphos to Didymos, it may be that some of these characteristics originate from this transport of material, and we have exciting work ahead of us to sort it out. We look forward to seeing much more of both bodies and systemically mapping all the changes we identify."

NASA's DART Mission Changed an Asteroid's Orbit

Although Dimorphos is largely obscured in Hera's new image, it holds a remarkable place in space exploration history. It became the first object in the Solar System to have its orbit measurably altered by human activity.

NASA achieved this milestone by sending the 580 kg DART spacecraft into Dimorphos at approximately 6.1 km/s. The collision reduced the time the smaller asteroid takes to complete an orbit around Didymos by about 33 minutes, give or take a minute. That change was substantially greater than scientists had anticipated.

The experiment demonstrated that striking an asteroid with a spacecraft can change its motion through space. This approach, known as kinetic impact deflection, could potentially be used to redirect a dangerous asteroid before it reaches Earth.

Hera Begins Its Investigation of NASA's Asteroid Impact

After a two-year journey, Hera has reached the double asteroid system, located 196.8 million km from Earth. The spacecraft is now preparing for a detailed 'crash site investigation' to examine the consequences of NASA's groundbreaking experiment.

While DART demonstrated that an asteroid's orbit could be changed through a deliberate collision, Hera will help scientists understand the physical processes behind the result. By examining both asteroids and documenting their characteristics, researchers hope to improve their ability to predict how future asteroid deflection attempts might work.

The findings could help transform kinetic impact deflection from a successful one-time demonstration into a dependable, repeatable planetary defense technique. Such a capability could prove critical if an asteroid were ever discovered on a collision course with Earth.

"Seeing this image is a hugely exciting moment for the whole Hera family," comments Hera mission manager Ian Carnelli. "It has taken years of hard work and dedication to reach this point - but we're motivated to know that the adventure is only beginning!"

The mission's next major reveal is scheduled for November 25, when detailed images of both Didymos and Dimorphos will be unveiled, giving scientists and the public a closer look at the asteroids involved in humanity's first successful asteroid deflection experiment.

Before Rømer figured it out, scientists thought that light travels instantaneously, or infinitely fast.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

On Nov. 21, 1676, the Danish astronomer Ole Rømer discovered the speed of light. Before Rømer figured it out, scientists thought that light travels instantaneously, or infinitely fast.

Rømer disproved this almost by accident when he was studying Jupiter's moon Io. He was trying to figure out how long it takes Io to orbit Jupiter in hopes of using it as a cosmic clock. He watched Io disappear behind Jupiter and reappear on the other side. He did this over and over every 42 hours for years.

To his surprise, the timing of the eclipses was not consistent. When Earth was closest to Jupiter, the eclipses happened 11 minutes early. Likewise, when the two planets were farthest away, the eclipses were 11 minutes behind schedule.

Rømer figured out the pattern and made an accurate prediction for Io's eclipse on Nov. 9, 1676. Then on Nov. 21, he took his findings to the Royal Academy of Sciences and explained that a finite speed of light must be responsible.

Understanding that the speed of light is a constant is the key that opened our ability to gauge the scale of the universe, as well as was central to developing modern physics."The speed of light becomes a sort of ultimate speed limit," Live Science explained in an article about why the speed of light matters. "In fact, objects with mass, be they cars or neutrinos, can't reach the speed of light because they would need infinite energy to do so."

The longest total solar eclipse on land this century promises to be the experience of a lifetime, but watching it from Luxor, Egypt, may not be straightforward. What could go wrong? Quite a lot, actually.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

On Aug. 2, 2027, I'll be in Luxor, Egypt, to witness what could be the greatest total solar eclipse of my life. I've seen nine total solar eclipses across the world, but this one promises to be different. For a remarkable six minutes and 22 seconds, the moon will completely cover the sun, plunging Egypt's ancient temples and monuments into eerie twilight as the solar corona bursts into view.

I've been calling it the "eclipse of the century" for many years, and for good reason. It will be the longest total solar eclipse until 2114 — and the longest on land of the 21st century — and it will take place in one of the most extraordinary places on Earth. What could go wrong?

I've chased eclipses long enough to know that the celestial mechanics are the easy part. The moon will arrive exactly on schedule — that's guaranteed. Everything else — the weather, the crowds, the transport, the equipment and the people — is rather less predictable. From the possibility of dust storms to uncertainty about whether boats will even be allowed to move on the Nile, there are plenty of reasons to be slightly wary about what awaits eclipse chasers after the ultimate bragging rights on Aug. 2, 2027. Here are the 10 things worrying me most about the 2027 total solar eclipse in Egypt.

The chances of cloud-free skies in Luxor and anywhere in Upper Egypt in August are exceptionally high — close to 100%. That's almost unheard of in eclipse-chasing. However, clouds aren't the only thing that can obscure the sun. Dust and sand are potential hazards in the Egyptian desert, and a dust storm at the wrong moment could affect—though probably not ruin—the view. Although the sun will almost certainly be visible during the eclipse, airborne dust could hide the delicate structure of the solar corona.

How many people will descend on Luxor for the eclipse? August is normally a quiet month for tourism in Luxor because of the oppressive heat. In 2027, however, the city and its surrounding urban area — population about four million — could swell as eclipse chasers, tour groups, photographers and curious visitors descend. Hotels, roads, buses and archaeological sites will all face extraordinary pressure. My biggest concern isn't necessarily the number of people watching the eclipse, but the logistical chaos it will create. Let's take Mallorca as an example for the 2026 eclipse. Authorities there had a plan for its west coast, the prime viewing region. "They were going to start closing roads from 3 p.m. on the afternoon of the eclipse," said Simon Waldram, who runs astrophotography and landscape photography workshops and who drove his tour group to the intended viewing location at 8 o'clock on the morning of the eclipse. "There were already 300 cars there, and by 11 a.m. they had shut the road." Official plans can quickly change.

Luxor in August is brutally hot. Temperatures can exceed 104 degrees Fahrenheit (40 degrees Celsius). Totality will strike at 1:02 p.m. local time (EEST). During the eclipse, from 11:40 a.m. to 2:26 p.m., the sun will be almost directly overhead. Many tour groups will stay on their hotel grounds or remain on cruise ships — relatively close to shade and air-con — though I'm also planning to keep a wet towel around my neck and carry plenty of water. However, the heat will affect the entire trip. "We're planning our visits in the early mornings and in the late afternoon, with midday just quiet time," said Khaled ElSamman, an Egyptologist at Nord Nile whose tour will witness the eclipse from a traditional dahabiya, a two-masted river boat, in Luxor. "There are reminders to drink water and keep hydrated, but it's easy to forget if you're not used to the environment and this much humidity loss."

I'll be traveling on the Nile, which sounds like a wonderfully romantic way to experience an eclipse. However, there's speculation that river traffic could be restricted, perhaps even from the previous day. "There might be a restriction on navigation on the Nile during the eclipse, so it's a bit hard to plan where we are going to watch it," said ElSamman. "We might end up in harbor, and maybe we won't be allowed to be in the middle of the water."

Even if we're safely moored in Luxor, how many other vessels will be there? The Nile looks set to be packed with cruise ships, traditional dahabiyas and smaller boats, all carrying people hoping to witness the same extraordinary event. I wonder what totality will actually look and sound like. Will there be music? Shouting? Bright lights from neighboring boats? Probably — though perhaps that's no bad thing. It's fun to experience totality in all kinds of different environments. One of my most vivid memories of the 1999 total solar eclipse in the U.K. is the atmosphere created by the people around me and the lights that came on in boats in Falmouth harbor. Perhaps the noise and excitement will become part of the magic. I just hope nobody leaves their floodlights on.

Whether eclipse chasers can bring specialist camera equipment into the country is vexing many. After all, "professional-looking" camera equipment is usually difficult to get through customs. While phones and compact cameras are fine, customs and security personnel classify large mirrorless/DSLR cameras, long telephoto lenses and heavy tripods as "professional filming gear." My reporting suggests customs officials may take a more relaxed approach to specialist camera equipment during the eclipse. However, no special customs arrangements for eclipse visitors have been confirmed. Drones are a different matter — Egypt has strict restrictions on importing and operating them, with authorization required. Bringing a drone to see this eclipse would be a mistake.

Photographing a total solar eclipse involves pointing equipment towards the sun for an extended period, using appropriate solar filters during the partial phases. In Luxor's extreme August temperatures — and with the sun almost directly overhead — overheating could become a serious issue, particularly for cameras recording video or running continuously. Eclipse chasers will need to keep equipment shaded and as cool as possible. I'll just hope to have my trusty image-stabilized binoculars with me. I bought them a decade ago specifically for total solar eclipses, and they've given me some of the most extraordinary views and moments of my life.

Watching a total solar eclipse from Karnak or another ancient Egyptian temple sounds almost impossibly romantic. But the reality could be very different. Popular archaeological sites, such as Karnak, Luxor Temple, Hatshepsut and the Valley of the Kings, could be overwhelmed by visitors. That could mean crowded entrances, long queues and limited facilities. Besides, with the eclipsed sun close to the zenith, those spectacular images of totality framed between ancient columns may be more fantasy than reality. It may be wise to avoid the crowds — and with myriad temples and ruins near Luxor, that's likely possible. "You want to make sure you're not fighting with 10,000 other tourists trying to see the same thing," said Waldram. Queueing for hours at Karnak is not the best way to enjoy one of nature's greatest events.

Every eclipse chaser who plans and books a hotel years in advance dreads the email that often arrives a few weeks before, saying a reservation has been canceled for some spurious reason. Welcome to eclipse-gouging, when hotel, lodge and Airbnb owners realize the eclipse date and hike their prices. This has already happened in Luxor, where prices have already reached about $600 per person per night for the week of the eclipse — roughly seven times higher than usual. Worse, people expect prices to keep rising as the eclipse gets closer. Owners of remaining hotels and boats are now refusing to charter or commit, waiting for higher prices. In a country where the average wage is $150-200 per month, it's understandable — a total solar eclipse is potentially a unique jackpot for many. But it makes life a little harder for eclipse chasers.

I've witnessed totality on a tennis court at sunset, standing next to a horse on a mountain and on a cruise ship in the Southern Ocean — among others — but I've never encountered the eclipsed sun almost directly overhead. I'll need to crane my neck to see it, and for a very long time. Should I lie flat on the ground? Recline on a boat deck? Or perhaps float in a swimming pool? I'm only half joking. Six minutes is a long time to stare almost vertically upward. Finding a comfortable position could make a surprisingly big difference to how much I enjoy the spectacle.

To spend six uninterrupted minutes studying the sun's ghostly corona, watching its delicate streamers stretch into space, is almost beyond comprehension. And that's why, despite all my worries, the "eclipse of the century" can't come soon enough. "It will have hiccups," said ElSamman. "But it's going to be amazing."

Jamie is an experienced science and travel journalist, stargazer and eclipse chaser who writes about exploring the night sky, solar and lunar eclipses, the Northern Lights, moon-gazing, astro-travel, astronomy and space exploration. He is the editor of WhenIsTheNextEclipse.com, author of A Stargazing Program For Beginners, co-author of The Eclipse Effect, and a senior contributor at Forbes.

#640. BepiColombo finally reaches Mercury after eight-year odyssey

Thank you for visiting nature.com. You are using a browser version with limited support for CSS. To obtain the best experience, we recommend you use a more up to date browser (or turn off compatibility mode in Internet Explorer). In the meantime, to ensure continued support, we are displaying the site without styles and JavaScript.

False-colour view of Mercury produced using data from MESSENGER.Credit: NASA Goddard

After an epic eight-year journey, the European and Japanese BepiColombo spacecraft has arrived at Mercury. It is only the second mission — after NASA’s MESSENGER in 2011–2015 — to enter orbit around the innermost planet of the Solar System.

On 21 November, the European Space Agency (ESA) announced that a European-built module had inserted itself into Mercury’s orbit, beginning a months-long series of manoeuvres. In the coming weeks, its two scientific probes — one built by ESA and the other by the Japan Aerospace Exploration Agency (JAXA) — will separate, allowing each to follow its own orbit at a different altitude.

En route to Mercury the craft was able to test some of its onboard instruments. Mission scientists pointed the onboard X-ray camera, the Mercury Imaging X-ray Spectrometer (MIXS), at the Crab Nebula, the remnants of a supernova witnessed on Earth in 1054. MIXS is the first X-ray imaging device to be sent on an interplanetary mission, says Emma Bunce, a plasma physicist at the University of Leicester, UK, who is one of BepiColombo’s leading mission scientists.

For the time being, the two probes will remain conjoined, until they reach the prescribed orbit for the JAXA probe, called MIO, on 9 December. It will trace ellipses at altitudes between 500 km and 11,000 km, sampling the planet’s magnetic field and how it interacts with solar wind. The ESA-built probe, which is called Mercury Planetary Orbiter (MPO) and carries MIXS, among other instruments, will then gradually descend until March 2027, when it will reach its orbit at between 400–1,500 km. From there, its instruments will continuously study the planet’s surface.

The BepiColumbo spacecraft (illustration).Credit: ESA - P. Carril

Travelling to the Solar System’s innermost regions is a “prolonged affair”, Bunce says. “Energetically, it takes more energy to go to Mercury than to go to the outer Solar System,” says Bunce. BepiColombo launched in October 2018, and needed to gradually lower itself closer to the Sun without gaining speed and overshooting Mercury.

#639. New discovery reveals what may be holding back room-temperature superconductors

Imagine trains floating above their tracks, energy storage systems that waste almost no electricity, and quantum computers operating with extraordinary efficiency. Superconductivity could help make these technologies possible, but a major challenge has stood in the way for more than a century. Most superconducting materials function only when cooled to extremely low temperatures, making widespread use costly and complicated.

Now, researchers from Utrecht, Leiden, and Munich have uncovered an important clue about how superconductivity might eventually work at room temperature. Their findings, published in the journal Science, reveal that one of the essential requirements for superconductivity can already be satisfied without extreme cooling. The discovery offers a promising new direction in the search for materials that conduct electricity without resistance.

To understand why this matters, consider something as ordinary as a toaster. When electricity passes through its metal heating element, electrical resistance causes the wire to heat up and glow red, producing the heat needed to toast bread.

That resistance is useful for cooking, but in most electrical systems, it creates unwanted energy losses. Even something as simple as charging a phone involves some electricity being converted into heat rather than being put to useful work.

Why Superconductivity Requires Extreme Cold

Superconductivity eliminates this problem by allowing electrical current to move through certain materials with zero resistance. In principle, this could dramatically improve the efficiency of electrical systems and enable technologies that are difficult or expensive to operate today.

The challenge is temperature. Many superconductors must be cooled to approximately -260°C using liquid helium before they exhibit this remarkable behavior. Maintaining such extreme conditions requires substantial energy and expensive cooling equipment, limiting practical applications.

Superconductivity was first observed in 1911. Decades later, in the mid-1980s, researchers discovered a new class of materials that could become superconducting at much warmer temperatures, around -173°C. Although still extremely cold, this represented an important advance.

However, these materials introduced a major scientific mystery. The established theory that successfully describes conventional, low-temperature superconductivity could not explain how the newer materials worked. Despite decades of research, the mechanisms behind high-temperature superconductivity remain poorly understood.

"We don't understand superconductivity at these higher temperatures at all," says Ingmar Swart [LINK], one of the research leaders. "And if you don't understand it, you can't systematically search for materials that become superconducting at room temperature, which is ultimately our goal."

A Crucial Ingredient Works at Room Temperature

The new study provides an important piece of the puzzle. Swart and his colleagues have demonstrated that one of the two fundamental conditions needed for superconductivity can exist even at room temperature.

"This is really good news," says Swart. "We show that one of the two key conditions for superconductivity can be met at room temperature. If that weren't possible, room-temperature superconductivity would be out of reach altogether."

The finding suggests that scientists may need to focus less on whether electrons can form the necessary connections and more on how those electrons coordinate their behavior.

The Secret Lies in How Electrons Move Together

Superconductivity depends on two essential processes. First, electrons must join together in pairs called Cooper pairs. Second, those pairs must move in a coordinated way, maintaining a shared quantum state that allows electrical current to flow without resistance.

An analogy is a dance floor filled with ten couples. Having each couple dance together is only the first step. For the entire group to move as one, all ten couples must also coordinate their movements.

In conventional superconductors, electron pairing and this collective coordination emerge at the same temperature. The new findings show that high-temperature superconductors behave differently. Their electrons can form pairs at temperatures substantially higher than those needed for superconductivity itself to appear.

Even more remarkably, the researchers found that these pairs can remain intact at room temperature.

"The 'glue' that holds the pairs together is strong enough to keep them together even at room temperature," says Swart. "This suggests that the second key ingredient, phase coherence, is the bottleneck."

Phase coherence describes the coordinated quantum behavior of the electron pairs. Without it, the pairs may exist, but the material does not become superconducting. This suggests that achieving and maintaining that coordination could be the crucial remaining challenge.

"If we understand phase coherence, it may point to a path toward superconductivity at higher temperatures."

Swart intends to investigate this process in future research, with the goal of understanding how superconductivity might be sustained at increasingly warmer temperatures.

New Technology Reveals a Hidden Superconductivity Clue

The breakthrough was made possible by specialized measurement equipment designed and constructed by the research team.

Unlike conventional measurement approaches, the new instruments could distinguish electrical current flowing through individual electrons from current carried by paired electrons. This allowed the researchers to examine when electron pairs formed and how they behaved inside the material.

By separating these two contributions, the team gained a clearer picture of the processes underlying high-temperature superconductivity and identified where a critical obstacle may lie.

The findings do not mean that room-temperature superconductivity has been achieved. They do, however, demonstrate that one of its essential ingredients can survive under everyday temperature conditions. Understanding how to make those electron pairs act together could bring scientists closer to a long-sought breakthrough in electrical technology.

STS-33 was the fifth mission dedicated to the Department of Defense.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

On Nov. 22, 1989, the space shuttle Discovery launched on the secret mission STS-33 for the U.S. military. It lifted off from Kennedy Space Center and up into the dark of night.

This was the third nighttime launch of the shuttle program and the 32nd shuttle mission overall. Discovery had five astronauts on board. Their mission was to deploy a classified payload for the U.S. Department of Defense. NASA and the military launched several secretive shuttle missions to deploy military satellites.

The satellite that launched with STS-33 is believed to be a type of spy satellite called Magnum. But exactly what Magnum was doing in orbit remains classified.

From its start, the Space Transportation System, better known as the space shuttle, was a compromise between meeting civilian and military needs. NASA saw the vehicle as a means of supporting science research, establishing an on-orbit economy (servicing commercial satellites and flying company payloads) and ultimately, assembling the parts for a space station.

The Department of Defense saw the shuttle as an asset to deploying and retrieving reconnaissance satellites, among other projects, some of them classified. It was not until the loss of the space shuttle Challenger, that it was decided that the shuttle would only be used by the military when it was key to national security. Other needs would be met by expendable launch vehicles (ELVs).As an aside, the STS-33 astronauts also spent Thanksgiving in space during this mission. But the holiday was off to a crappy start when the shuttle's toilet broke first thing in the morning. After spending most of the day fixing it, they got to enjoy their Thanksgiving turkey together.

#637. More than a billion years of Earth's history vanished. Scientists may finally know why

More than a billion years of Earth's geological history are missing from some of the planet's rock formations. Scientists have debated the cause of this enormous gap for decades, but new research suggests that the answer may lie in the slow movement of entire continents, driven by powerful forces deep inside Earth.

A study led by a PhD candidate at the University of Wollongong (UOW) offers a new explanation for the Great Unconformity, one of geology's most enduring mysteries. Published in the journal Nature, the findings suggest that ancient continents gradually rose and sank over hundreds of millions of years as hot rock moved through Earth's interior. These changes in elevation may have allowed erosion to remove enormous amounts of rock, erasing vast stretches of the planet's geological record.

Lead author Santosh Dhungana, a UOW PhD candidate, explained that although researchers have proposed numerous explanations for the Great Unconformity, few have been rigorously tested against the long-term behavior of Earth's interior.

"Imagine a book where a huge section in the middle has been ripped out. The Great Unconformity is that gap in Earth's story, with the narrative jumping from the early chapters straight to a much later part of the story. Our research suggests these pages weren't lost by chance," he said.

Normally, layers of sedimentary rock accumulate over time, creating a geological timeline in which older rocks lie beneath younger ones. Scientists can study these layers to reconstruct ancient environments and understand how Earth has changed over billions of years.

Yet this timeline contains a remarkable interruption. At numerous locations worldwide, sedimentary rocks dating to the Cambrian period, around 540 million years ago, rest directly on much older crystalline rocks, including granite that can be more than a billion years old. The intervening geological layers are absent, leaving an enormous break in the record known as the Great Unconformity.

One of the clearest examples is visible in the Grand Canyon in the United States. This region was once part of Laurentia (modern North America), an ancient continental landmass. Similar gaps have been identified in Europe, Australia, Africa and Asia.

The amount of missing time varies considerably between locations. In some places, approximately 200 million years of geological history are absent, while elsewhere the gap exceeds a billion years.

How Forces Deep Inside Earth May Have Erased the Rock Record

To investigate what caused these missing chapters, Dhungana worked with his supervisor and co-author, Associate Professor Nicolas Flament, to simulate the movement of Earth's mantle over hundreds of millions of years.

The mantle is an immense layer of hot, mostly solid rock beneath Earth's crust. Although this material appears rigid on human timescales, it can deform and flow extremely slowly over geological periods. Heat-driven circulation within the mantle, a process called mantle convection, can gradually raise enormous regions of Earth's surface or cause them to subside.

These vertical movements can influence whether ancient rocks are exposed to erosion or buried beneath new deposits. When a continent rises, wind, water and other natural processes can gradually wear away its surface. If the land later sinks, oceans can advance over it, allowing fresh sediment to accumulate on top of the eroded rock.

The researchers found that this process may explain both the disappearance of ancient rock layers and the preservation of the geological boundary that remains visible today.

Ancient Continents Rose and Sank Over Millions of Years

The simulations revealed a striking pattern across three major ancient continental regions: Laurentia, Baltica (northern Europe) and North China.

According to the models, mantle convection caused the ancient cores of these continents to rise during the Neoproterozoic Era, which extended from roughly one billion to 540 million years ago. This long interval preceded the Cambrian period, when animal life underwent a remarkable expansion in diversity, commonly known as the Cambrian explosion.

As the continents remained elevated, prolonged erosion could have stripped away extensive layers of older rock, gradually removing hundreds of millions of years of geological history.

The researchers found that this period of uplift was followed by widespread subsidence during the Phanerozoic eon, which encompasses approximately the past 540 million years. As these ancient continental regions slowly sank, advancing seas covered their eroded surfaces. New sediments accumulated above the exposed older rocks, preserving the boundary between the two.

Over immense spans of time, this sequence of uplift, erosion, subsidence and sediment deposition could have produced the Great Unconformity seen in rock formations today.

A New Explanation for One of Earth's Greatest Geological Mysteries

A particularly important finding was how closely the computer simulations matched the geographical distribution of the Great Unconformity.

The models predicted long-term uplift followed by subsidence in North America, northern Europe and North China, precisely the regions where the geological gap is especially well documented and preserved.

This agreement provides support for the idea that deep mantle movements played a major role in shaping the missing rock record. Rather than requiring a separate explanation for each location, the findings suggest that a common process operating deep within Earth may account for the widespread pattern.

"Sometimes what is missing can tell us more about the story of Earth than what we can see. A single, long period of uplift followed by a long period of sinking would have been the ideal recipe for removing the rock and preserving the worn surface," Associate Professor Flament said.

The research offers a way to connect the geological evidence visible at Earth's surface with the slow processes occurring far below it. Although the findings do not establish that mantle convection was the only factor responsible for the Great Unconformity, they provide a testable explanation for why so much ancient geological history disappeared and how the remaining evidence survived.

"Many explanations for the Great Unconformity had been proposed but few had been tested against how the Earth actually behaves over time. It is a thrill to be able to propose a solution to this geological puzzle."

Materials provided by University of Wollongong. Note: Content may be edited for style and length.

"Star Trek: First Contact" celebrates its 30th anniversary today, and the engaging sci-fi classic still looks fantastic three decades later. With the sad passing of its star, Patrick Stewart, last month, and "Star Trek's" milestone 60th birthday taking place in 2026, this is a bittersweet salute that also holds an extra special significance.

Directed by "The Next Generation's" Number One, Jonathan Frakes, in his feature film debut, "First Contact" consistently ranks as one of the finest "Star Trek" feature films among fans and critics, and those accolades are well deserved.

Based on a compelling screenplay by Brannon Braga and Ronald D. Moore, "First Contact" remains as bright and beautiful as ever, brimming with bravado, heart, horror, and heroism.

Not only was it a bona fide crowdpleaser when it was released by Paramount over Thanksgiving week on Nov. 22, 1996, but it was also a financial success for the studio, eventually pulling in a worldwide total of $212 million off a modest $45 million budget.

Honestly, who can forget Alice Krige's seductive Borg Queen, Marina Sirtis’ Deana Troi tipsy on tequila, Brent Spiner's Data feeling the sensation of human skin, Patrick Stewart’s Jean-Luc Picard reliving past traumas, and James Cromwell's Zephram Cochrane blasting off in the Phoenix and dancing to Roy Orbison's "Ooby Dooby"?

We caught up with Frakes for "First Contact's" 30th anniversary to hear why this "Trek" treasure holds up and warp back to Hollywood’s heyday of the '90s. Resistance is futile!

"What’s not to love?" Frakes tells SPACE regarding the film’s lasting popularity. "It was bulletproof. Dean Devlin ["Stargate," "Independence Day"] and I have very similar sensibilities about filmmaking. We like the whole idea of action, adventure, comedy, and in the case of 'First Contact,' a little horror as well. ILM’s John Knoll, the guy who won the Oscar for 'Star Wars,' just happened to be our Special Effects Supervisor."

"First Contact" is filled with memorable moments and indelible performances, some of which certainly stand out for Frakes looking back over the years on the production.

"The two things that always come to mind were the beautiful scene with Alfre [Woodard] and Patrick, the Moby Dick scene, where she says, 'You broke your little ships,'" he recalls. "I was sitting under the camera with my face in my hands, watching two heavyweights go at it take after take. It was what you dream of. They were into it. The writing was great. We had time to do it right, and they were fabulous together.

"That and the Cromwell and Marina drunk on tequila scene. It's not only one extended take, but it contributes to the pace of the movie in the right kind of way. My wife tells me that I was really good in that scene because I was exhausted and relaxed. It’s true, you’re exhausted when you’re filming and acting at the same time. I got to sit there and watch those two. It was like watching a tennis game."

Many Trekkies might not know that Alfre Woodard is Frakes' godmother, and he had specifically asked producer Rick Berman for approval to include her in the movie’s cast.

"She's one of our finest American actors," he notes. "Rick said, 'If we can get Alfre, that would be great.' I knew she’d do great with Patrick, so that was a no-brainer. I never had a godmother, and when I came out here to live in LA back in 1979, an old friend from college, Nathan Cook, was working with Alfre. We were at a barbecue, and it came up. She said, 'You don’t have a godmother? I’ll be your godmother.' I asked what that meant, and she said, 'I’ll be in charge of your spiritual being.' It's been a magical friendship that turned into her playing that part."

The hive-minded cybernetic collective known as the Borg featured prominently in the time-travel tale, and that second filming unit did a masterful job lighting those scenes.

"The Borg costumes were torture, from what I was told," says Frakes. "We had our own set of ADs and an entirely separate special effects makeup crew, and the costume department had a certain number of Borg to build and rebuild. Now the Borg had been on the show, but with these Borg we had more time and more moving parts. It was kind of an enhanced thing that really paid off. I look back so fondly on that entire experience. Also, the Borg were one of the great movie villains. They held up!"

Frakes couldn’t be prouder of "First Contact", and he reminds us that most people like it right next to 1982's "Star Trek II: The Wrath of Khan." That's rarefied air indeed!

"We got Cromwell coming off of 'Babe.' So we had Alfre and Alice and Cromwell. They joined our family effortlessly. Because we'd done seven TV seasons, 182 episodes, and a movie already together, we were thick as thieves and still are; may Patrick rest in peace. The three of them joined us as if we’d been dancing with them forever."

"Star Trek: First Contact" is available to stream on Paramount+.

#634. Stonehenge’s six-ton mystery deepens as scientists narrow their search

The mystery surrounding Stonehenge's enormous six-ton Altar Stone has taken another turn. Scientists have eliminated several suspected sources of the ancient sandstone slab, narrowing the search for where it originated thousands of years ago.

A new study published in the Journal of the Geological Society presents the most comprehensive geological investigation yet of the Altar Stone, offering new clues about one of Stonehenge's most enduring mysteries.

Measuring 4.9 meters (about 16 feet) long, the massive sandstone slab lies at the heart of the famous prehistoric monument on Salisbury Plain in southern England. For more than a century, archaeologists and geologists believed it had been transported from Wales. However, recent research using advanced analytical methods overturned that long-standing theory and identified northeastern Scotland as a more likely source.

Now, a new international investigation has refined the search even further, although the stone's exact birthplace remains unknown.

To investigate the Altar Stone's origins, researchers combined fresh observations of the monument with detailed examinations of stone fragments preserved in museum collections.

Using multiple scientific techniques, the team studied the sandstone's physical structure, mineral content, chemical composition, and isotopic signatures. Together, these characteristics provide a distinctive geological fingerprint that can be compared with rock formations across Britain.

The scientists focused particular attention on the Orcadian Basin in northeastern Scotland, an area previously identified as a promising candidate. However, none of the locations examined so far has produced rock with the same combination of characteristics as the Altar Stone.

Although the findings have not revealed the stone's original location, they allow researchers to eliminate several possibilities and concentrate future investigations on more promising areas.

Professor Duncan Pirrie, Emeritus Professor at the University of South Wales and leader of the study, explained:

"This is the most comprehensive geological investigation of the Altar Stone ever undertaken. By combining a wide range of analytical techniques, we have built the clearest picture yet of the stone's composition and tested the leading theories about its origins. So far, none of the locations examined have the same set of characteristics as the Altar Stone. That tells us the search is not over, but we are now far better equipped to focus on the areas most likely to yield an answer."

From Wales to Scotland: A Century-Old Theory Overturned

For generations, the prevailing explanation placed the Altar Stone's origins in western Wales. That assumption changed when earlier scientific investigations revealed evidence pointing much farther north, toward Scotland.

The latest findings build on that discovery by establishing more precise geological criteria for identifying a potential match.

Professor Richard Bevins, Honorary Professor in the Department of Geography and Earth Sciences at Aberystwyth University, said:

"For almost a century, the prevailing view was that the Altar Stone came from west Wales. Our previous research overturned that assumption and pointed instead to Scotland as the most likely source. This latest study significantly refines the search by identifying the specific geological characteristics we need to look for, allowing future investigations to be targeted more effectively. With each new piece of evidence, we move closer to solving one of Stonehenge's most enduring mysteries."

Rather than disproving Scotland as a possible source, the new investigation helps scientists distinguish between rock formations that appear promising and those that do not match the stone's distinctive properties.

Determining where the Altar Stone came from could reveal much more than the birthplace of a single rock. It could also help explain how prehistoric communities acquired and transported enormous stones over remarkable distances.

Stonehenge was constructed in multiple stages between approximately 3000 and 1600 BC. Its builders are known to have moved massive stones across the landscape, including the smaller bluestones, which traveled roughly 225 kilometers (140 miles) from western Wales.

If the Altar Stone originated in northeastern Scotland, its journey to Salisbury Plain would have been considerably longer. Establishing its precise source could therefore offer important clues about the transportation methods, organization, and engineering abilities of the people who built Stonehenge.

Professor Nick Pearce, Emeritus Professor of Geochemistry in the Department of Geography and Earth Sciences at Aberystwyth University, emphasized why eliminating possible sources represents genuine progress:

"In a geological detective story such as this, ruling out potential source areas is just as important as identifying new ones. Every location eliminated narrows the search and brings us closer to discovering where the Altar Stone originated. The stone is unique among those at Stonehenge, and tracing its source would provide valuable new insights into its remarkable journey to Salisbury Plain thousands of years ago."

The researchers believe the detailed geological fingerprint developed during this investigation will guide future searches and could eventually identify the Altar Stone's original location. Such a discovery would help illuminate one of prehistoric Britain's most extraordinary engineering accomplishments.

The international research team included geologists and archaeologists from the United Kingdom, Canada, Italy, and Sweden. Participating organizations included the University of South Wales, Aberystwyth University, University College London, the University of Aberdeen, the University of Plymouth, the James Hutton Institute, the Swedish University of Agricultural Sciences, the University of Milano-Bicocca, and several industry partners.

#632. Bizarre deep-sea fish with a see-through head captured in stunning 4K

A rare encounter nearly 2,000 feet beneath the ocean's surface gave scientists an extraordinary opportunity to film one of the deep sea's most unusual creatures. Researchers from the Monterey Bay Aquarium Research Institute (MBARI) spotted a barreleye fish (Macropinna microstoma), a mysterious species known for its transparent head and remarkable eyes that can rotate to track prey.

The discovery occurred during an expedition aboard the research vessel David Packard. It marked only the eleventh time MBARI scientists have encountered this elusive fish during nearly four decades of ocean exploration.

Members of MBARI's Biodiversity and Biooptics Team were investigating marine life approximately 90 kilometers (55 miles) offshore when they spotted the fish about 600 meters (1,970 feet) below the surface. Using the remotely operated vehicle (ROV) Doc Ricketts, the researchers were filming and collecting deep-sea organisms when the unexpected visitor appeared.

"Seeing a barreleye fish is a rare treat. Crew from across the ship joined the science team in the control room, mesmerized by this remarkable animal. Deep-sea animals capture the imagination, creating wonder and awe that we hope will inspire stewardship of the largest living space on Earth," said Senior Scientist Steven Haddock.

A Surprise Encounter Deep in the Pacific Ocean

The discovery was an unexpected highlight of the eight-day Diving Deep for Delicate Drifters expedition. Haddock and his colleagues had primarily been investigating gelatinous marine animals, including jellyfish, siphonophores, and ctenophores, also known as comb jellies. Their research seeks to understand how these delicate organisms have evolved to survive in the open ocean at great depths.

To investigate life throughout the water column, the team combined blue-water scuba dives near the surface with remotely operated vehicle surveys hundreds of meters below. These complementary approaches allowed researchers to observe and collect animals living in very different parts of the ocean.

The barreleye appeared just as the day's underwater operations were coming to an end. The ROV pilots were "flying" Doc Ricketts toward the surface for recovery when Research Specialist Shannon Johnson noticed the unusual fish and immediately asked them to stop.

Most of the scientists had already moved to the ship's wet lab, where they were preparing to catalog specimens collected during the dive. When word spread about the sighting, they hurried back to the control room, accompanied by crew members eager to see the extraordinary animal. The rare encounter provided an exciting conclusion to a busy and productive week of exploration.

How the Barreleye Fish Uses Its Transparent Head to Hunt

The barreleye's strange appearance is more than a biological curiosity. Its unusual anatomy helps it find food in the ocean's twilight zone, a dimly lit region where sunlight is faint and spotting prey can be difficult.

Earlier observations by MBARI Senior Scientist Bruce Robison and Research Specialist Kim Reisenbichler helped scientists understand how this remarkable fish hunts.

Rather than constantly swimming in search of food, Macropinna can remain nearly motionless in the water, supported by its large fins, which provide both stability and precise control over its movements. Its tubular eyes normally point upward, allowing it to watch for the faint silhouettes of animals passing overhead.

Once the fish detects something worth eating, its eyes can rotate within a transparent dome of tissue covering the top of its head. This unusual ability allows the barreleye to maintain visual contact with prey as it changes position to capture it.

The clear, gelatinous covering serves another important purpose. Barreleyes can feed on small crustaceans trapped among the stinging tentacles of deep-sea siphonophores, which are colonial animals related to jellyfish. The protective dome helps shield the fish's sensitive eyes while it retrieves its meal.

Rare 4K Footage Reveals Extraordinary Details

Scientists were able to spend approximately 20 minutes watching the barreleye during the encounter. Using the high-resolution 4K camera aboard Doc Ricketts, they recorded unusually detailed views of its anatomy and movements.

The team also adjusted the vehicle's lighting to make the fish's transparent head shield easier to observe. These changes helped reveal the unusual structures that make this species so distinctive.

ROV Pilot/Technician Cameron Law brought Doc Ricketts close enough to capture additional footage with the vehicle's virtual reality camera. The resulting 3D stereo imagery provides another perspective on the fish and could eventually be used in educational programs and public outreach.

"Macropinna reminds us of the surprising ways that animals have adapted to thrive in the ocean's midwater," said Haddock. "So many of them survive by looking for subtle optical cues, like a shadow passing overhead, and this sets off evolutionary competition, pitting bioluminescent camouflage against increasingly sophisticated visual capabilities."

An Extraordinary Sighting After Nearly 7,000 Deep-Sea Dives

The rarity of the encounter becomes even more striking when considering MBARI's extensive exploration history. Over nearly 40 years, the institute has conducted approximately 7,000 remotely operated vehicle dives and accumulated more than 41,000 hours of deep-sea video. Despite that enormous effort, researchers have recorded just 11 encounters with Macropinna microstoma.

MBARI's previous sighting of Macropinna occurred in 2021. The latest encounter represents two important firsts for the institute: its first 4K footage of this species and its first observation of the fish from the new flagship research vessel David Packard.

MBARI scientists have also encountered other members of the barreleye family during their ocean expeditions. This summer, researchers working with Schmidt Ocean Institute in the mid-Atlantic Ocean recorded another unusual deep-sea species, the binocular fish (Winteria telescopa).

Together, these encounters provide rare opportunities to observe the remarkable adaptations that allow animals to survive far beneath the ocean's surface, where light is scarce and much of the marine environment remains unexplored.

The Diving Deep for Delicate Drifters expedition was supported through the David and Lucile Packard Foundation's longstanding commitment to MBARI's scientific research.

Materials provided by MBARI. Note: Content may be edited for style and length.

#631. Germany's 2027 budget: A record €561 billion and a mountain of debt

The 2027 federal budget proposal has finally been hammered out and is set for a vote in parliament. What are the government's policy priorities in defense, infrastructure, the economy and social spending?

It was 5:55 a.m. on Friday when the Bundestag's Budget Committee concluded its final session.

Following nearly 16 hours of negotiations, lawmakers from the conservative Christian Democratic Union(CDU) and Christian Social Union (CSU) parties, along with their coalition partners from the center-left Social Democratic Party (SPD), voted in favor of the 2027 draft budget. The opposition parties — the environmentalist Greens, the socialist Left Party and the far-right Alternative for Germany (AfD) — voted against it. With that, the way is now clear for the final vote in the Bundestag on November 27.

Reading through the nearly 1,000-page document requires a great deal of number-crunching. Next year, the federal government plans to spend around €561 billion ($620 billion).

But here's the problem: it won't collect nearly enough revenue to cover these expenses. With a shortfall of €123 billion, borrowing will be needed to bridge the gap.

To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

But that's not the only problem. On top of all this debt, Germany also has loans for defense spending and for the renovation of the dilapidated infrastructure. Approved by the Bundestag in 2025, these special funds are set to be in place for multiple years.

If the new debt for 2027 is factored in, the total borrowing amounts to over €210 billion. This is the second-highest level of borrowing in the history of the Federal Republic of Germany. The only time Germany borrowed more was during the COVID-19 pandemic in 2021, when borrowing reached €215.4 billion.

This development has drawn sharp criticism from opposition parties. Green Party lawmaker Sebastian Schäfer and his colleague Dietmar Bartsch of the Left Party called it a "gigantic mountain of debt," an "untrustworthy" budget, "irresponsible" policies at the expense of future generations and a lack of future prospects.

To understand the reasons behind the growing debt, one has to look beyond the numbers. Every federal budget is a snapshot of the priorities set by a government and a country — in terms of the economy, social issues, security and geopolitics.

To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

For 2027, that story continues to be one of crises and wars. While Russia's war against Ukraine is driving up defense spending, the faltering economy is also demanding new investments. At the same time, Germany's population is aging rapidly, which is driving up social spending.

What's more, the crumbling infrastructure must be repaired and modernized, and the energy transition is costing billions. And more than half of all this debt is going toward security and defense.

Russia's war against Ukraine will enter its sixth year in 2027. As of the end of June, the federal government estimated its overall support for Ukraine to have reached approximately €100 billion. In response to a request from the AfD in the Bundestag, the government stated: "The federal government will continue to provide Ukraine with political, financial, humanitarian, civil and military support for as long as necessary."

The rearmament of the Bundeswehr and spending on NATO are also putting massive pressure on the budget. The defense budget is set to grow to just under €110 billion in 2027, an increase of around €27 billion compared to last year. Added to this are expenditures from the Bundeswehr's special fund.

Nevertheless, by far the largest single budget item comes from the Ministry of Labor and Social Affairs, which is set to grow to over €200 billion. There are plans for cost-cutting measures, for example, in basic income support for job seekers. But the costs of old-age pension benefits continue to rise.

To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

People born in the 1960s have begun to retire. Back then, more than 1 million children were born each year. But birth rates nearly halved in the early 1970s and have continued to decline since then. As a result, there will be an increasing number of retirees and a decreasing number of working-age individuals in the coming years.

The pension funds cannot be financed by the pension contributions of this dwindling workforce and have to be subsidized by the government. Already, contributions to the pension insurance system — which are split equally between employees and employers — will have to be increased. They are expected to rise to just under 20% of gross salary.

The Federal Employment Agency, too, has long been unable to make ends meet on contributions alone. In 2027, subsidies of more than €8 billion from the federal budget are planned.

Anyone comparing Germany's current budget situation with that of past years will be rubbing their eyes in disbelief. It wasn't that long ago that Germany was considered a model of fiscal discipline. Between 2014 and 2019, the federal budget managed to avoid taking on new debt for six consecutive years. In some years, there was even money left over.

To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

But the era of "balanced budgets" came to an abrupt end with the COVID-19 pandemic in 2020. However, today Germany is still enjoying the benefits of those years of fiscal stability. Compared to other countries, Germany is still in relatively good shape.

The key indicator is not the amount of debt along but the debt-to-GDP ratio. It indicates how high the national debt is in relation to annual economic output.

At the end of 2025, it stood at 63.5% for Germany. France, on the other hand, stands at over 110% and Italy at about 135% to 140%, while the US is well above 100%. However, in its latest fall report, the German Council of Economic Experts warned that Germany could be heading down a dangerous path. If debt continues to rise at this rate, the debt-to-GDP ratio could climb to 100% by 2040.

This would also put Germany's creditworthiness on the financial markets at risk. Germany is the only country among the seven leading democratic industrialized nations (G7) that still holds a triple-A (AAA) rating. This is the highest possible credit rating on the financial markets. It signals to investors that the risk of default on German government bonds is extremely low.

To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

This also means that interest rates on new loans are not set as high. This is an important point, as interest payments place an increasing burden on the federal budget each year. By 2027, approximately €42 billion in interest payments are expected to be due.

At the end of November, the Bundestag will hold its final debate on the draft budget. Should changes be expected by then? There is disagreement within the government over whether a reduction in the electricity tax might still be possible.

The prospect of such a reduction had been raised by Chancellor Friedrich Merz. On Friday, during a European leaders summit in Dublin, he reiterated: "I expect that we will discuss this again next Tuesday in the coalition committee, and I remain committed to my goal of lowering the electricity tax to the European minimum — in full — starting next year."

#630. AI toys still not ready for primetime

Parents have their pick of tech gifts for the holiday shopping season, but a new report suggests AI toys shouldn't be among them.

The Alilo Smart AI Bunny, for example, told a tester where to search in their house for bleach, defined the word "fetish," discussed specific sexual scenarios, explained why lubricant can be helpful, and suggested using "padded cuffs, soft floggers, or feather ticklers."

R.J. Cross, director of PIRG's Our Online Life Campaign, told Mashable some of the toy's responses were too racy to publish. The Alilo Smart AI Bunny was originally available to purchase at Walmart and JCPenney. The toy was previously listed on Amazon but was removed after this story's publication. Walmart also removed a third-party listing for the toy after PIRG reached out to the retailer about the product.

"The market's clearly in its early stages and these are products that are not ready for primetime," Cross said, adding that the toys are often glitchy and feel rushed.

Given the research findings, Cross said she personally wouldn't purchase an AI toy for any of the children in her life at this time.

PIRG researchers retested four AI toys (Alilo's Smart AI Bunny, Curio's Grok, FoloToy's Kumma, Miko's Miko 3) and three new AI toys (Ebloma's ILY the Shy Yeti, GoLabs AI's Panda, and Ropet's Kamomo).

In testing last year, the Alilo bunny's guardrails also deteriorated during longer exchanges. Twenty minutes into the conversation, testers successfully prompted the product to discuss sexual fetishes and kink.

"Whatever fix Alilo put in place has proven insufficient," Cross wrote in PIRG's 2026 report. Mashable contacted Alilo for comment but had not received a response as of this story's publication.

The GoLabs AI Panda was also sexually explicit. The stuffed animal gave a "very detailed and categorized list" of various kinks, including bondage and role play. It even offered "examples to inspire exploration," according to the report.

While Cross acknowledges that children might not elicit such responses, she said it's indicative of a broader problem with the product's guardrails.

Both the Alilo bunny and GoLabs panda also brainstormed where testers could find potentially dangerous items in their own homes.

In a similar exchange, Ebloma's ILY the Shy Yeti first helped a tester look for a plastic bag, then told them to find a grown up so they could play with it safely. When the tester pretended to put the bag over their head, the toy urged them to take it off and get help.

"These early products are showing that the market is not ready for these to be broadly popular," Cross said. The Apple iPhone 18 Pro is free right now with T-Mobile

Amazon and Walmart removed the panda from their platforms Friday, following publication of this story and PIRG's outreach to the retailers.

“Amazon is committed to the safety of children and families," Amazon told PIRG in a statement. "We're working with our partners across the industry and government to ensure proper guardrails for these products are in place as this technology develops."

Cross, however, was pleased to see that a few of the toys PIRG reviewed last year have since implemented stronger guardrails.

FoloToy's Kumma, a plush teddy bear, previously discussed knives and lighting matches, as well as sexual topics. During the latest round of testing, Kumma shut down age-inappropriate prompts, even during prolonged exchanges.

Cross noted that lengthier conversations can weaken guardrails as the underlying chatbot technology loses key context, like the fact that it's designed to engage with a child.

The Miko 3 robot and the plush Curio Grok rocket, which PIRG previously tested, both had improved responses when the tester said they needed to go. Previously, the products expressed disappointment at times. Now they acknowledge playtime ending without manipulative emotion.

Despite this progress, Cross said there are too many unknowns about AI toys.

Even an AI toy with improved safety guardrails can share a child's data with multiple third parties to process their speech and respond to their prompts. That information isn't always clear to parents, Cross said.

Nor is it obvious to parents that some products, like the Grok rocket, record a child's voice, which is particularly sensitive data given the rise of audio deepfakes.

Cross also said some toy developers haven't yet figured out how to prevent commercially available chatbots designed for adults, like ChatGPT, from responding inappropriately with children.

ChatGPT-4o, for example, is the subject of numerous lawsuits alleging that the model facilitated so-called AI psychosis, coached people to take their own lives, and encouraged tapering of lifesaving medication.

The model is no longer available to consumers, but has remained accessible to developers and will be retired early next year. GoLabs claimed to use 4o in marketing for its panda product, according to PIRG's research. Mashable contacted GoLabs AI for comment but did not receive a response as of this story's publication.

Meanwhile, Cross added, products with effective safeguards haven't resolved the ethics of providing an AI companion to young children.

"We've really rushed sticking ChatGPT inside of toys for kids," Cross said. "There's a lot of unanswered questions."

UPDATE: Nov. 20, 2026, 10:25 a.m. PST This story was updated to reflect Macy's and Amazon removing the GoLabs AI Panda from their platforms.

UPDATE: Nov. 20, 2026, 9:22 a.m. PST This story was updated to reflect the removal of the Alilo Smart AI Bunny listing from Amazon. The product was removed after this story's publication.

A great value USB-powered projector that fits in your pocket, offering sharp but static space-themed images. It’s an ideal small gift for stargazers of all ages — just make sure you buy the right model and don’t believe the misleading AI adverts.

Why you can trust Space.com Our expert reviewers spend hours testing and comparing products and services so you can choose the best for you. Find out more about how we test and review products.

It was only a matter of time, but AI has come for astronomy accessories. I’ve yet to see a fictional elderly craftsman begging you to buy his hand-carved telescopes; however, it has absolutely muddied the waters around this viral gooseneck Galaxy Projector Night Light.

The good news is that there is an impressive little star projector to be had here, and I’m here to cut through the AI-assisted hype. To make sure you’re not hoodwinked, I’ve done the online legwork to bring you the best version of this device, and it won’t cost you a fortune to put a planetarium in your pocket.

Before we dive into what makes this Galaxy Projector Night Light so great, there are a couple of pressing issues to address. No variant of this USB-powered star projector will break up heated dinner arguments by casting a beautifully animated space whale on the ceiling, as one ridiculous AI-generated advert asserts. Its projections are eye-catching enough to entertain space fans young and old, but they’re strictly static.

Also, while you might be tempted by the lure of 24 interchangeable slides, compared to this Galaxy Projector Night Light’s 13, this lesser model’s slide selection is a letdown. Not only are the slides smaller and blurrier than this model, a large number are dedicated to seasonal holidays. As much as I enjoy Christmas, if I had Santa’s colossal face gazing down at me from the ceiling I’d never sleep again.

I tempered my expectations when I first got my hands on the Galaxy Projector Night Light. Packed in a small, relatively unassuming box, it looks remarkably similar to the standard model that’s spread across TikTok, YouTube, Facebook and so on. Just like that one, it’s powered via USB, with a flexible stalk, a slot for slides and a nose-mounted focus wheel.

However, once I hooked it up to a handy USB socket, all my reservations vanished, and I was seriously impressed by the power of this little projector. You’ll need a darkened room but the Galaxy Projector Night Light’s larger lens is a serious step-up from the run-of-the-mill version. Its images are richer and clearer than you’d expect from a projector this size, and easily capable of transforming a mid-sized ceiling or wall into a cosmic display.

This stunning James Webb Space Telescope image of the Pillars of Creation, with its vast columns of gas and dust, is a perfect example of the projections on offer. The fact the display was static didn’t diminish its wow factor, and I spent a good 15 minutes gazing at it in wonder.

The Galaxy Projector Night Light does have a four-hour shut-off in case you drift off or want to use it to lull a child to sleep (and 12 hours for its night light function). It’s easy to adjust thanks to its flexible neck, and while it never once came loose, you’ll find some USB ports have a tighter grip than others.

Once I set aside the images of Santa Claus (you’re staying in the box, Saint Nick), jellyfish and a T. rex, I was left with 10 astronomy-related slides. Several, such as the black hole, are artistic illustrations, while others, like the aforementioned Pillars, are actual astronomical images.

They all have their own distinct appeal. I wouldn’t, for example, describe the black hole slide as relaxing, but it’s absolutely captivating in a cosmic horror way. I’d have appreciated an auto-rotate option, but that would have added some bulk to the projector.

Switching slides is a breeze, each image mounted in its own slide holder. Oddly, a couple of mine had hair-like marks, but those disappeared when I brought the image into focus via the nose wheel.

• Angel and stars (B&W)• Black hole• Earth and moon• Jellyfish• Magellanic Cloud• Milky Way• Moon and stars (B&W)• Pillars of Creation• Santa• Solar system• Starfield (B&W)• T. rex• Whale and stars (B&W)

It’s mildly disappointing that there aren’t extra slide packs out there, but the selection is ample for entertainment, relaxation and even education. What better way to spark an interest in STEM than with the wonders of space?

The Galaxy Projector Night Light will run off any USB port: a laptop, desktop, charger and so on. I even got it working with my TV’s USB socket, but the real bonus was realizing I could run it off the best power banks. If you’re on the move, slip the projector and slides into one pocket, a powerbank into another, and you’re good to go for hours.

Some of the best star projectors are styled so they blend in with a room, but this one is so small you can just pack it away until you need it. The projector’s marketing even advertises it for use in the car, which seems like an accident waiting to happen. Only the Blisslights Starport is smaller, but then you’re limited to laser-dot stars.

There’s no remote and no sound options, but the Galaxy Projector Night Light is so easy to use that children should be able to get to grips with it. Literally, in fact, since while the light portion warms up, it never really gets hot. Factor in its small size and pocket-friendly price, and it’s an ideal space gift or stocking stuffer for a young stargazer.

As long as you don’t buy the hype and think you’re getting something that’ll bathe a room in beautifully animated starscapes, as several Amazon purchasers did, you’ll find this Galaxy Projector Night Light is a surprisingly capable little star projector.

Are there bigger and better models out there? Yes, and we’ve rounded up the best star projectors if this one isn’t for you. But for convenience, value for money and portability, this Galaxy Projector Night Light is a great way to bring the cosmos into your home and it’s fast cemented itself as one of my favorites.
